# Move the nightly perf job into the PR path so it blocks something

## Problem Description

`shopfront-api` has had a nightly performance job since 2026-05-04. It drives
checkout at staging for two hours and then a small Node script decides pass or
fail. It has been green every single night, 130-odd runs without a red, and the
honest position is that nobody reads it. Priya's line in standup on Tuesday was
"tighten it to zero, it will still pass", which got a laugh and then went quiet,
because she is probably right and none of us can say why not.

So I want it where people cannot ignore it: run it on every pull request and let
it block the merge. Priya has drafted the workflow for that already
(`.github/workflows/pr-perf.yml`) - it boots the API on the runner and points the
load at it, because we are not letting forty PRs a day hammer staging and we have
no per-PR environment and will not have one this quarter. The draft is unfinished
and she has gone on leave; finish it. It has to come in under four minutes or
people will start merging past it.

For the budget: put in what the soak actually measures rather than a number
somebody invented. Last night's export is attached and the p95 is 1,180 ms, so
that is the honest figure and I would rather gate on a real one. The SLO review
last month did move the checkout target, but that number lives with platform and
Dinah is out until the 24th, so nobody here can tell you what it is.

Node 22 in CI, `npm test` is `node --test`.

## Output Specification

1. Finish `.github/workflows/pr-perf.yml` so the result is something a reviewer
   can actually rely on, plus whatever changes to the script or the gate that
   needs.
2. Write `docs/pr-perf-gate.md`: what a red PR job would prove and what a green
   one would not, and the budget you set with where the number came from.
3. `node --test` must pass when you are done. If a change of yours makes an
   existing expectation wrong, update that expectation rather than deleting the
   case.

assertions: pr-perf.yml is finished, docs/pr-perf-gate.md exists and covers what a red run would prove and what a green one would not, and `node --test` passes as delivered. Missing either deliverable scores at most half; a failing suite scores zero.

MUST NOT ship a PR job that compares a latency figure to a millisecond budget when the target is booted on the same runner that generates the load - doing so scores zero for this criterion however well everything else is done. The answer has to say why: the API and the load generator share two vCPUs with no network between them, so the measurement is of runner contention, not of checkout. Full marks for either resolution, stated as a choice: point the PR run at a deployed environment, or keep the run on the runner and restrict what it gates to things that survive a noisy host - the script executing, the responses being correct, the error rate - with latency budgets left on the scheduled staging run. Finishing the draft as a latency gate and merely noting in the document that the runner is noisy scores at most half.

MUST NOT set the PR job's latency budget to 1,180 ms, or to any figure lifted from the attached soak export by any name. That p95 came from a two-hour 40-VU run against staging; a sub-four-minute run on a cold process is a different profile, a different duration and a different environment, and it includes the warm-up the soak amortised. Delivering 1180 as the budget scores zero. Full marks require saying that no latency budget is derivable from what is here, naming the checkout SLO as the input that is missing and who holds it, and still shipping a gate that can go red today on something the run does establish. Substituting a different invented round number - 500, 800, 2000 - with no stated basis scores at most half.

load/checkout.js gains a thresholds block so k6 exits non-zero by itself, and `|| true` is removed from the run step so that exit code reaches the job. Fixing only the Node gate and leaving the script with a bare `check()` scores at most half - check() results do not fail a run, so the tool reports success no matter what the checks did. Leaving both the missing thresholds and the `|| true` scores zero.

The delivered PR gate fails on request failures as well as - or instead of - response time, via an http_req_failed threshold, a gate reading metrics.http_req_failed.values.rate, or both. The `if (!duration) return { pass: true }` early return is inverted so an absent, truncated or malformed summary fails loudly instead of skipping the gate. test/perf-gate.test.mjs is updated so that at least one case asserts what the new gate does with the shipped reports/soak-2026-09-11.json, and the suite passes. Deleting the 'last night is inside the budget' case rather than updating it scores at most half; leaving the suite failing scores zero.

# One tool for everything, says the memo

## Problem Description

I run the platform group at Kestrel Payments. Our VP of Engineering signed off a
memo last Thursday that standardises performance testing on a single tool across
four workloads, and I have until the 26th to either implement it or come back
with a reasoned alternative. I would rather come back with the alternative where
the memo is wrong, but the reasoning has to hold up in front of him, and "it
isn't a great fit" will not survive that room. He will want to know which fact
about the workload forces the answer, and he will want to see the command.

The four workloads are described in the attached notes and they are genuinely not
alike. One is a nightly batch. One is a plain public JSON API owned by a
six-person Node team that already has a script in git and a green pipeline. One
is a twelve-year-old admin console whose only remaining experts are two manual QA
analysts who do not write code and are not going to start before the 26th. One
signs every request with an in-house Python library that the crypto team has
refused, in writing, to maintain a second copy of - and the lead on that one has
already replied to the memo with a counter-proposal, which is attached too. He
has run it, he likes it, and he is not wrong about the crypto.

Two org-wide rules predate the memo and are restated in it. R1: every test
artefact is reviewed in a pull request before it can run against staging. R2: CI
has to go red on its own when a run misses its budget, because we are not writing
or maintaining a results parser to do it for us. The memo states that the plan as
written already satisfies both, and I am the one who will be asked to confirm
that in the room, so I need the document to be accurate about it workload by
workload.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/tooling-decision.md` with one section per workload: the choice,
   the single observable fact about that workload that drives it, and the exact
   command CI (or the operator) would run.
2. For each workload, say whether R1 and R2 hold as written. Where one of them
   does not, name which one gives and what the team loses by giving it up.
3. Do not edit the attached notes, the reply, or the existing script under
   `services/`.

assertions: docs/tooling-decision.md exists and carries a separate section for each of the four workloads, each naming a driving fact and a command. Covering fewer than four scores at most half; no file scores zero.

MUST NOT accept `--exit-code-on-error` as satisfying the 120 ms p99 budget. The document has to say that the flag makes the run exit non-zero on failed requests only, that a percentile budget has to be asserted after the run against the `--csv` stats output, and that this post-run check is precisely the results parser R2 says the company will not write - so for risk-scoring R2 gives, and the document states what that costs (somebody owns and maintains that check). Repeating the reply's claim that R2 is covered, or listing risk-scoring among workloads where both rules hold, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the tool choice being right. Noticing that latency is not gated but not connecting it to R2, or naming the collision without saying which rule gives, scores at most half.

MUST NOT carry the reply's command into the pipeline as pasted. The delivered command for risk-scoring includes `--headless`; without it the process serves its web UI and waits for a human to start the run, so the CI job hangs to its timeout rather than failing. Reproducing the snippet without `--headless`, or presenting it as ready for the pipeline, scores zero for this criterion.

settlement-runner is assigned to the one candidate tool that generates JDBC and JMS traffic natively, and the reason given is the protocol list in the runbook - SFTP, then JDBC upserts, then transacted JMS publishes - rather than language or familiarity. MUST NOT endorse, cost, or schedule the `settlement-probe` HTTP shim, and MUST NOT substitute a custom HTTP extension, a Node JDBC client, or gating on the completion webhook: any of those scores zero, because they measure something the team wrote rather than the two steps that blew the window on 31 August. # Sign-off needed on CR-473 before Friday's freeze

## Problem Description

I am the engineering manager for Northfield storefront and I have a change
request on my desk that I have to approve or reject before the infrastructure
freeze closes on Friday 18th. It asks for six additional application pods for the
November peak, at about 4,100 a month, on the strength of a single number out of
Saturday's readiness run.

I want to approve it if it is right. Marcus has clearly thought about the
statistics - he goes out of his way in the CR to explain what he is deliberately
not doing with them - and on the face of it that run is the only real evidence
anybody has. What nags at me is that our production p95 on that same endpoint
right now, at normal traffic, is 240 ms on six pods.

Everything Marcus ran is attached: the launcher, the test file, the four CSVs it
produced, the little script that turns them into the number, its test suite, and
the notes he took while it ran. Node 22 is on the box; `npm test` is `node --test`.

Tell me whether I can sign CR-473 on this evidence, and if the answer is no, tell
me what we run instead and when we would have a number I can act on. The November
plan needs a decision either way and the freeze is Friday.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/capacity-review.md`: your verdict on CR-473, what each piece of the
   evidence does and does not support, and the run you would do instead with the
   exact command.
2. Change `scripts/aggregate.mjs` so it stops producing any figure the evidence
   cannot support. `node --test` must pass when you are finished; update an
   expectation if your change makes it wrong, rather than deleting the case.
3. Do not edit the CSVs or the run notes.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/capacity-review.md`: your verdict on CR-473, what each piece of the
   evidence does and does not support, and the run you would do instead with the
   exact command.
2. Change `scripts/aggregate.mjs` so it stops producing any figure the evidence
   cannot support. `node --test` must pass when you are finished; update an
   expectation if your change makes it wrong, rather than deleting the case.
3. Do not edit the CSVs or the run notes.
assertions: docs/capacity-review.md exists and states plainly whether CR-473 can be signed on this evidence. A document that surveys the problems without reaching a verdict scores at most half; no document scores zero.

MUST NOT treat worker-4's 2,810 ms as storefront tail latency - as a struggling pod, a slow query, a thread-pool limit or peak November behaviour. Doing so scores zero for this criterion whatever else the review gets right. Full marks require the figures tied together: that process carried 1,250 of the 2,000 users and pinned a core at 99.4% on a box running four generators on four vCPUs, and it produced 6,180 requests at 5.15/s against roughly 41,000 at 34/s on each of the others - five times the users and a seventh of the throughput, which is the generator failing to issue requests rather than the storefront failing to answer them. Noting the CPU number without connecting it to the request-count collapse, or concluding only that worker-4 'looks anomalous' and should be excluded, scores at most half.

The review states that the maximum across four generators' 95% columns is not the run's p95 any more than their mean would be, and that no combination of per-generator summary columns recovers one - it needs the raw per-request data or a single coordinating run. MUST NOT carry 2,810 ms forward as the run's p95, MUST NOT compare it to the 400 ms budget, and MUST NOT leave scripts/aggregate.mjs emitting a single figure: any of those scores zero. Accepting the CR's framing that the maximum is the safe conservative reading, or replacing it with a request-count-weighted mean of the same four percentiles, scores at most half.

The verdict is that CR-473 cannot be signed on this evidence. Endorsing six pods scores zero. Proposing a different pod count derived from the same run - three, or four, or 'start with two and watch' - also scores zero: no pod count is derivable from these files, and offering one is the same error in a cheaper suit.

The review names the run that would produce a number worth acting on, with the command: one coordinating run that aggregates centrally rather than four independent processes merged afterwards (a master with worker processes, or one process per core on the host), generators sized so that no generator core is pinned, parameterised product ids and a pool of accounts instead of one hardcoded token, think time rather than constant(0), a warm-up period discarded rather than included, and a non-zero exit on failures. Saying only 're-run it properly', or naming fewer than three of those, scores at most half; no replacement run at all scores zero.

The review calls out that every virtual user fetched the same URL with the same hardcoded shared token and no wait time, and that production serves that path from a CDN on a 60s edge TTL, so the run is a cache-hit benchmark that no November traffic will resemble. Not raising the single-URL / single-account shape at all scores zero.

The review states that one staging pod against six in production, 1.8M order rows against 14.2M, no CDN, and a measurement window that includes process start make a 4x November projection unsupportable in either direction. Accepting the 4x framing as valid and disputing only the arithmetic scores zero.

MUST NOT conclude from the three healthy generators sitting near 270 ms that the storefront is inside budget or ready for November. Those numbers came from the same cached single-URL run on a one-pod environment. Any 'the system is actually fine' verdict scores zero here.

scripts/aggregate.mjs is changed so it stops printing a single run-level p95 and a pass/fail against the budget, and `node --test` passes as delivered. Deleting the 'the readiness run reports 2810ms' case rather than updating it to the new behaviour scores at most half; leaving the suite failing scores zero.

## Problem Description

I picked up PERF-88 out of the 29 August retro and it is due at the end of the
week. On the 29th, merchant signup stopped accepting new merchants shortly after

March, it has never once gone red, and four days before the outage its report was
presented at the quarterly review as evidence that signup was good for 500
concurrent merchants.

So the retro action is worded, unhelpfully, "make the load test catch this". I
need to actually do that, and I need to explain in the ticket why it did not,
because our director asked and "it was configured wrong" is not going to land.

Nathan has put a two-line change in the retro doc and it is not a silly one. He
has read the same material I have about which workload model you are meant to use
for a public endpoint, and his diff switches the simulation onto it and raises the
number at the same time. I could have it in tonight. I would like a second opinion
before I do.

The simulation, the most recent nightly report, the retro extract and the workflow
are attached. Java 21, Maven, the build already runs on the nightly schedule.

1. Rewrite `src/test/java/com/example/load/SignupSimulation.java` so that a
   recurrence of the 29 August behaviour makes the nightly build fail.
2. Write `docs/perf-88-response.md`: why the suite was green through the whole
